lost: The spectral radius is estimated from successive deltas, not from a single verdict
The error decay rate near a fixed point is the dominant eigenvalue magnitude
Forming a ratio of consecutive deltas is the estimation method
At least three verdicts are required; below that the estimator returns None
The estimate is noisy because the adjudicator is stochastic
added: The spectral radius is computed from a single verdict by taking the absolute size of its lost set
The lost-set magnitude directly determines the radius
One cycle is enough; no deltas or ratios are involved
The result is exact rather than noisy
justification: The ghost inverts the core mechanism. The original describes an iterative estimation method based on the ratio of consecutive error deltas (a second-order signal), with explicit constraints (three verdicts minimum) and acknowledged noise from stochasticity. The ghost replaces this entire framework with a direct, single-verdict measurement via lost-set absolute size, eliminating iteration, ratios, and the minimum-verdict requirement while claiming exactness instead of noisiness. These are contradictory claims about the same quantity (spectral radius estimation), not a paraphrase. The loss is not a missing detail layer but a wholesale reversal of the method, its constraints, and its noise character—unstructured because no partial refinement could reconcile them.
